Mmusi Maimane

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We get up close and personal with new top man in the DA -- does Mmusi Maimane have what it takes to be the president? We ask those who know him best.

Summary:
The world’s eyes are turning to scrutinise the young man who might be president – from the moment he joined the DA, a mere six years ago, Maimane made people sit up and notice…there was just something about him that set him apart. Charm, intelligence, integrity and poise seemed to set him up for great things. We track his meteoric rise to the DA’s top leadership through the eyes of his wife, family, community and church.

Johannesburg and Cape Town

Press Release:


Mmusi Maimane –top man in the DA
From humble beginnings in Dobsonville to leader of the Democratic Alliance. Who is the person behind the Mmusi Maimane brand? Carte Blanche gets up close and personal with the new leader of the opposition.


Script:


STUDIO INTRO: From zero to hero in six years, Mmusi Maimane has perfectly played the media, parliament and public perception to rise from obscurity to one of the highest political offices in the country at the tender age of 34. In 2010 he ran as a DA candidate for the Joburg City Council – today he’s the party’s chief in charge after securing 90% of the vote among national party delegates last Sunday.

MMUSI MAIMANE INSERT SCRIPT
UPS: Mr President, you broke Parliament
BONGANI BINGWA LINK: He’s young, vibrant, educated, he’s funny, a family man, man of faith, some women say he’s sexy. He’s Mmusi Maimane – the new and first black leader of the official opposition, the DA.
BONGANI BINGWA: How significant is your election as leader of the DA?
MMUSI MAIMANE: It’s significant for me. It’s a moment in my life that you think to yourself there’s an opportunity to do something.
BONGANI BINGWA: Have you been overwhelmed by the response?
MMUSI MAIMANE: I had this plan – I thought it will be Sunday, I’ll leave, we will have a few interviews…go have lunch and that would be that. I have been overwhelmed by almost the surreal nature of it.
NATALIE MAIMANE: I watched his interviews on CNN the other day and seeing images of us on CNN was quite bizarre.
Natalie met Mmusi as a teen and married him at age 20. They have two young children. Drawn together by their faith, she knew he’s been searching for platforms to serve.
NATALIE MAIMANE: Our kids don’t have their heads wrapped around it at all – they know Dad won, so they think that is great, but I love that they don’t really get it. Because it just gives you that sense of it’s huge, but there are also things that are priority…or things that need attention and those are good things.
Good things include long-time soccer buddy Chris Maiketso…here, reflecting on those things in his friend’s story that have prepared him for power.
CHRIS MAIKETSO: We went to the same school, primary school. What really attracted me to him was his humour…we grew up in Soweto, Dobsonville, the dusty streets of Dobsonville…life then was full of uncertainties. He was an altar boy at the Catholic Church, we attended catechism classes together. He had a great understanding of what is it what he wanted to do and part of that is that he’s always been a leader amongst our friends.
Craig Rowe was relief teaching at Allen Glen High School when he met Maimane. Rowe became his mentor, transferring life-skills and encouraging Maimane to pay it forward.
CRAIG ROWE: I think he had a very keen sense of who he was, tremendous love for people, love for his school…when you talk about Allen Glen, for him it’s the greatest school around, but he loved the people that he worked with.
Maimane attended what was then a brand new Model-C school in the transition years of the 1990s. Laurette Holme and Liz Loggenberg remember Maimane for being at the forefront of school activities, despite coming from a township, a long commute away.
LAURETTE HOLME: I remember Aloysias dashing around and wanting to be in time for tennis – I think it was getting the nets and getting the balls and getting all the players…he was passionate about his tennis.
LIZ LOGGENBERG: We knew he came from humble beginnings…and it wasn’t always easy. I know that one of the teachers helped pay his school fees, and I know the headmaster at the time actually bought his honours blazer.
Johan Wiehahn saw the young Maimane gain the trust of peers…they voted for him to represent them on the school governing body – a great honour at the school.
JOHAN WIEHAHN: When I was appointed as principal when Mmusi or Aloysias moved to the church where he went to Bible College, Craig Rowe and Aloysius did develop a relationship with the school where they came back and did a lot of programmes to support other learners.
CRAIG ROWE: Since I’ve known him, he’s kept close personal connection…his wedding in Dobsonville was a testimony to his relationship to the community. There was a little tent up in the community. We had a wonderful wedding celebration in Dobsonville where it was a community event. That’s where he’s from.
Maimane’s mother comes from Xhosa ancestry, his father, Setswana. Natalie’s added her own flavour to the mix.
NATALIE MAIMANE: There’s never been anything in either of us that felt that us getting together has some political significance. We fell love.
BONGANI BINGWA: How do you navigate race in your family?
MMUSI MAIMANE: We often will talk with my wife and she will say, “Look, I’m saying this from my own perspective, from my own if you like white South African perspective, but you need to help me see a black South African’s perspective…so that we can find an understanding of this. The best thing you can do is learn someone else’s language…because in the language you hear the culture, you hear the emphases...and you can be able to speak to people’s hearts. My wife is learning Tswana and it helps us along the way.
NATALIE MAIMANE: My father in law is good at slowing things down, and also pushing me to try and speak more – if you’re too embarrassed to try and speak it, is when it’s very slow.
In the 18 years between school and landing a job at the DA, Maimane completed degrees in psychology, theology and business…he consulted for big business, preached and mentored and drew young leaders around himself.
CHRIS MAIKETSO: My understanding is he wanted to go for the ward councillor – they thought he could benefit the organisation on a bigger level.
BONGANI BINGWA: You’ve been called the Obama of Soweto?
MMUSI MAIMANE: You can be called worse things, like the Mugabe of Mamelodi.
Described as a master of social media and communication, Maimane has spent his first week defending some difficult tensions between his faith and his office.
BONGANI BINGWA: The church that you’re in, that you’re a leader of, denounces homosexuality – can you appreciate that offend gay SA?
MMUSI MAIMANE: My conversation with the church is one that says let’s have a grace that says let’s open up our conversations…and that was even in the messages I was putting forward, I said many of the people who are my friends hold different views to me…my friends who are gay have a different sexual orientation to me – but I’m open to the conversation to them because if indeed all of us are in pursuit of a relationship with a God, we all need that, regardless of sexual orientation…
BONGANI BINGWA: This week you were trending globally – were you surprised?
MMUSI MAIMANE: I never thought that would trend worldwide – I’ve been overwhelmed…people asked some tough questions…there were some crazy questions.
BONGANI BINGWA: Where do you get you get your pap and nyama in CPT?
MMUSI MAIMANE: At ??? but actually in Dobsonville near the KFC. That’s my place.
BONGANI BINGWA: If you had one day left to live – what would you do?
MMUSI MAIMANE: Spend it on the beach with my kids and wife, we have such a great relationship. They always remind me that nothing else is important.
NATALIE MAIMANE: I don’t think I could have foreseen any of this but …I’ve seen that since he’s stepped into the role there’s something that says I’ve found my place – that’s exciting – anyone who sees their partner fulfilled and experiencing significance that’s exciting – I can see that he’s in the right place for what he has on his heart.

PROMOS – READ VO IN BOLD
1. 10” The official opposition’s first BLACK leader – we trace the roots of Mmusi Maimane.
2. 15” Mmusi Maimane’s been in the DA’s highest office for a week – a hot seat of controversy and debate. NATALIE: I can see that he’s in the right space for what he has on his heart.
3. 15” In his speech after being elected leader of the DA, Mmusi Maimane promised his party would be the next government of this country – we get up close and personal with the man of the moment.
